sources.citation: Ford, Lysbeth Julie. 1998. A Description of the Emmi Language of the Northern Territory of Australia. PhD thesis, Australian National University. 474 pp. hdl:1885/10796 (open access).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Each phonological word has a distinctive stress pattern in that its initial syllable is raised in pitch and is thereby prominent. The initial syllable bears primary stress ... Every third (odd-numbered) syllable thereafter carries secondary stress, e.g. padjarranba [ˈpaɟaˌranba] "parrotfish"; demiwulytjiwulytji [ˈdɛmɪˌwuʎcɪˌwuʎci] "kidneys". The final syllable of a polysyllabic word is unstressed, e.g. ngammama [ˈŋam.ama] "deaf"; pitjawakatj [ˈpicaˌwakac]. Enclitic particles never bear stress.' Also (pp.70-73): coverbs and incorporated nominals inside the verb complex bear secondary stress on
sources.locator: sec. 2.3.2 'Word-stress', p.70 (PDF p.94); identity Ami=Emmi at sec. 1.1 p.1 ('Earlier writers refer to the language as Ami')
sources.note: The only reference grammar of Ami/Emmi, with a dedicated word-stress section (2.3.2, p.70); our classification rests on a 1970 sketch of a different language (Maranungku). downloaded now; it confirms initial primary stress but states the final syllable is never stressed, so the record's odd-parity rhythm strings (101, 10101) are wrong for Emmi.
